Chapter one · The crossing

George Downard.
Another shore.

27 December 1821 – 12 June 1902

Before there was a Downard family in Utah, there was a family in England willing to leave nearly everything familiar behind. In 1862, George Downard, his wife Sarah Ann, and their children joined a Latter-day Saint migration across the Atlantic. Their destination was not simply America. It was a distant gathering place in the mountain West.

They sailed from Liverpool aboard the William Tapscott, a large emigrant ship that departed on 14 May 1862 and reached New York on 25 June. The crossing lasted roughly six weeks. Crowded shared quarters, unfamiliar food, seasickness, religious fellowship, and the uncertainty of arrival were common features of emigrant voyages; the precise experience of the Downards is not recorded in a surviving diary known to us.

An atmospheric illustration of the William Tapscott voyage—not a portrait of the actual ship.
A name almost lost

The manifest says Dowrard.

The voyage index transcribes George's surname as Dowrard, rather than Downard. The variation matters: a researcher searching only the modern spelling could overlook the family's crossing altogether.

Earlier English parish entries also used Downward. These may reflect changing historical usage, handwriting, or transcription; the original records should be compared before calling every difference a clerk's mistake.

George's passenger entry ↗ · Voyage record ↗

14 May 1862Departed Liverpool
25 June 1862Arrived New York
19 October 1862Wagon company reached Utah

Their ocean crossing was only the beginning. George's family continued west with the Horton D. Haight wagon company. Family research reports that their infant son Edward Hirum died during the overland journey. The ship transcription names an infant Edmund Dowrard. See the unresolved identification. This loss sits at the heart of the migration story: the promise of a new home came at a terrible personal cost.

Church migration was often financed through pooled resources, personal borrowing, and the Perpetual Emigrating Fund, which helped eligible converts travel with an expectation of repayment. Family research suggests that George's household incurred migration-related debt. Until an original account or ledger is identified, however, we cannot state exactly who advanced the money, how much was owed, or when it was repaid.

A family crossed the sea looking toward a new life. One of their children would never see the valley they hoped to call home.
A new life in Utah

A home, then another beginning.

George settled in Utah and later married Mary Emma Carlisle in Spring City in 1865. Their son John Louis was born in 1869. George's life crossed the worlds of English craft work, Mormon migration, and settlement in territorial Utah.

His obituary and the family's reported movements between Sanpete and Carbon counties offer promising leads for a fuller account of his work, faith, and community. The surviving newspaper text should be checked against its original page before specific anecdotes are presented as fact.

Illustrative Utah landscape; not a historical photograph of George's property.
Archive image from the family research collection, labeled George Downard. Names, dates, and relationships should be verified against the original record.
Chapter two · A life in the West

John Louis
Downard.

6 September 1869 – 23 September 1944

John Louis was born in Spring City, Utah, just seven years after his father George crossed the ocean. The difference between their childhoods is striking: George grew up in nineteenth-century England; John Louis knew the towns, ranches, and changing frontiers of Utah.

John married Angelina Rebecca King in Price in 1896. Their children included Manual Louis, Walter William, and a daughter, Angelina. After Angelina's death in 1913, John later married Minnie Estella Thompson Rogers and Gertie Elenor Miller.

The old newspapers do not always preserve a whole life. Sometimes they preserve the day everything changed.

In August 1913, a newspaper account described the accidental shooting that killed Angelina near Woodside. The family account involves a revolver that fell as a nephew handled a holster. This is a painful part of the family's history and deserves careful, respectful treatment—not sensationalism. The original clipping and its date should accompany the full account when recovered.

John's death record contains a particularly important genealogical puzzle: his mother is reportedly identified as “Hanna Ann Hicks,” a name associated instead with Angelina King's family. The record may contain an informant error. We preserve the discrepancy rather than silently replacing the recorded name.

John Louis Downard: death record from the family archive. A primary record can preserve both valuable evidence and mistakes.
Research note. The relationship of John Louis to George and Mary Emma is supported by compiled family material, but conflicting parent information on his death certificate should be shown alongside other evidence rather than erased.
Chapter three · The house next door

Walter William
& Clace.

Walter 1899–1975 · Clace 1895–1989

Walter William Downard, John Louis and Angelina's son, was born in 1899. He married Clace Sabey in 1921. Their family story stretches from rural Utah to the neighborhoods of Vernal, where family houses, gardens, and everyday routines became the backdrop of childhood memories.

Clace had three daughters from an earlier marriage to Marshall McKinley Bradley. With Walter, she had Thomas John and Delores “Nancy” Downard. Distinguishing Walter's children from his stepchildren matters: a family tree is most useful when it records relationships as they actually were.

Records and family recollections place the family in Altonah, Bingham Canyon, and Vernal over the decades. Newspaper notices document financial and legal difficulties in the 1950s, but they are only fragments of a much longer life.

“Grandma D was the salt of the earth. Gruff but that was only show.”
— Robert T. Downard, family journal

Clace's grandson remembered a woman of modest means who held her family together. Other recollections evoke an apricot tree, sugar cubes, Saltine crackers, and the little rituals that made her house feel familiar. These details are not grand historical events. They are precisely what turns genealogy into memory.

Walter William Downard: a historical record from the family collection.
Unresolved detail. Family sources differ on Walter and Clace's exact September 1921 marriage date. The original certificate should settle it.
Chapter four · The Mugg

Thomas John
Downard.

3 December 1921 – 22 May 1982

Thomas John Downard was born in Bluebell, Utah, in 1921. He married Norma Lucille Lambson in Salt Lake City on June 26, 1942, as the world was at war. Family record. Their life together would encompass military service, hard work, children, baseball diamonds, and the enduring rhythms of Vernal.

Thomas served in the U.S. Army's 136th Infantry Regiment, 33rd Infantry Division, with service in Alaska and the Pacific during the Second World War. After the war he worked in mining and oil fields, at Ford, and for the U.S. Postal Service, where family history credits him with thirty-one years of service.

He coached baseball and helped build local diamonds. To the people who knew him, he was more than his occupations and dates. He was “The Mugg,” a man remembered through stories that are funny, affectionate, and wonderfully specific.

Some people leave monuments. Others leave stories that are told every time the family gathers.
Small things remembered

The purple bags. The roasting pan. The folded bill.

Family memories tell of coins kept in purple bags, a missing roasting pan pressed into service for an unexpected burial, and a folded hundred-dollar bill offered when someone might need help. These stories reveal a personality more vividly than a list of addresses ever could.

Thomas and Norma raised three sons: Robert T., Glenn L., and Quinn C. Their story is part of the larger Downard family history, but it is also the beginning of the memories carried by their children and grandchildren.

A soft, illustrative evocation of Utah; family photographs can replace this artwork.
Historical family document supplied during research. Its subject and provenance should be confirmed before publication as a labeled ancestor record.
Chapter five · A memory of home

Robert T.
Downard.

12 September 1948 – 13 February 2009

Robert T. Downard was born in Vernal in 1948, the son of Thomas John and Norma. He inherited a family story that began, in Utah, with a difficult ocean crossing nearly a century earlier. Yet some of his most revealing words look not toward distant history but toward the grandmother he knew.

In a family journal, Robert described Clace—“Grandma D”—as frugal, outwardly gruff, and deeply loving. He remembered that she kept the family together. It is a rare gift when an ancestor leaves behind their own words about an earlier generation: one life briefly illuminates another.

“She would do anything for me, but I seldom asked. She kept the family together. I have nothing but fond memories of her.”
— Robert T. Downard, remembering Clace

Robert died in 2009. This chapter closes the direct line followed in this telling, but not the story itself. Five generations after George left England, the Downard name had become inseparable from Utah places, people, and ordinary acts of care.

Family archive document. Additional identification and verification are needed before assigning it definitively to Robert T. Downard.
End of this edition. This website intentionally stops with Robert T. Downard. It does not publish identifying details about living descendants.
Notes from the archive

What survives. What we still seek.

This is a narrative mockup built from family research and historical records. Dates, relationships, and memories are identified as reported where original verification remains outstanding. The drawings are atmospheric illustrations; the documents are scans supplied for family research.

  1. Saints by Sea: William Tapscott voyage, 1862 and George “Dowrard” passenger entry.
  2. Church History Biographical Database: George Downard and Horton D. Haight company migration records.
  3. Family-supplied Utah death records, contemporary newspaper excerpts, and the journal recollections of Robert T. Downard.
  4. Open questions: original emigration debt ledger; George's complete obituary; the original 1913 Woodside article; corroboration of several family relationships and dates.

The earlier English generations, including Thomas Downward, Elizabeth Edwards, William and Kitty Welch, are intentionally outside this edition's starting point.
